utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, are you rising for a reason or merely to be ready for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's deal with the both.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first procedural issue that I have relates to the e-mail that I received late last night from my colleague Chester Stamp that has to do with inappropriate and unlawful access to certain witnesses, as colleague Chester Stamp put it in the mail, and to me, that sounded very serious, so I replied immediately to Mr. Stamp and requested that he explain what exactly he was referring to, so that I could do whatever it takes and whatever is necessary on my side to take measures to remove any unlawfulness in accessing witnesses. I also received a reply from my Colleague Stamp that I saw this morning which eased my mind, but on the other hand, I think this issue has to be resolved and cannot be delayed, and therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's okay, but something is with connection. [Interpretation] So I believe that this issue should -- deserves to be brought to the attention of this Trial Chamber before the summer recess. And in connection with that, I wonder if we can expect some more detailed information regarding the claims that Mr. Stamp put in his e-mail. But I just have to note, to mention, that the witness -- that the Defence team is very aware of what their rights are and how they can access and talk to the witnesses called by the Prosecution. What I can say is that the Defence never, no member of our team spoke with any witness in any way that would be unlawful and that would be in contradiction of the rules. We know that if we want to interview a witness who has already provided a statement to the Prosecution, we may do so only with the approval and presence of our colleagues. So we are completely clear on that. And if the Trial Chamber has something -- can shed some more light on this or issue some further instruction, I will very gladly hear them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have only very recently been given some information about the problem that is perceived, and there is an e-mail, I think, from Mr. Stamp, a statement of the normal and appropriate procedure which appears to be consistent with that which you are putting. And if that is all that has occurred, it does not appear that there should be any problem. It did appear, though, from an e-mail of Mr. Stamp, that there may have been approaches, if not by a member of the Defence team, it seems to be suggested that approaches by a person acting in the interests of the Defence, a person who had a senior position of authority in the police force. At the moment, the Chamber has no way of knowing what the facts might be other than the e-mails which have passed between the parties. Can I suggest that if there is more which needs to be considered, that that be specifically raised on the part of the Prosecution, and that issue can then be considered after we've heard from you, Mr. Djordjevic. At the moment, we will proceed on the basis that both sides understand the normal proper orthodox procedure to be followed, each are aware of it, and each will be doing all they can to ensure that that is observed. Now, if there is more, we will hear. If no more is raised, we will understand the matter has been dealt with by this exchange just now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Baccard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. I would remind you the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Djordjevic is finishing his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. This will not take very long. We just need to clarify some matters that the Defence wanted to clear up. We talked yesterday about the Cirez site, let me remind you, and in that respect, the last thing we discussed was the blood haemolysis, or rather, the dissolution of blood in water, and the period which was mentioned, the period of time of 2 and a half months. My learned colleague Visnjic, when you testified in the Milutinovic case, when he asked a similar question that had to do with both the blood and other bodily fluids, and rather, putrefaction fluids - and this was on page 10.178 - you replied that that depended where the blood was found preserved, whether it was on the inside of the body or on the surface or some other place. Now, here the blood that was found with the two bodies for which it was supposed that they had been sexually assaulted, it is stated that the traces of blood were found on the vulva. Now, Doctor, would you agree with me this in that case that would mean that this blood was on an external surface, that it wasn't in any body cavity.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask you for permission to consult my report once again because I believe that the reference to traces of blood is mentioned in relation to a cutaneous excreation and therefore the interpretation must be done in relationship to this superficial wound, but if I may, I'd like to consult my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, please confirm your recollection by looking at your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the Court Officer please pull up document 65 ter 00206, the French and English versions without the B/C/S version. Yes, this is the document. Could we now display page -- or rather, the page that refers to Cirez site. I believe that's on page 6 in the English version, and I am afraid I don't have the French reference. But in English that's page 6. Probably it's on the same page in the French version as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, can you please peruse this as well in the meantime, and the matter that we were discussing was also in your addendum of May 23rd, 2002, as you stated. This is just to remind you what I'm referring to. You requested that you be allowed to look at this to refresh your memory, and then I expect you to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I did not personally see these corpses. It was on the basis of information that was given to me, that is, the reports that had been prepared by the forensic specialist and the photographs that had been given to me that I made this -- that I drafted this report. There were two victim, one called SIPC 1, and SIPC 2. And in both cases, there was -- they presented red blood at the vulva opening, and in addition there were signs of violent trauma in the genital area, close to the genital area. And these were abrasions, superficial wounds of the skin, with blood at that area. In the case of SIP1C 1 and in the case of SIP1C 2, the same findings had been made by the forensic specialist, that is, the presence of blood at the vulva opening, and also traces of violent trauma of -- on the right thigh and the left leg. The mention of blood was not my own. This was something noticed by the forensic specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for your reply. We already have that information, but what I would want to know, my first question, if you notice traces of red blood, was this external blood, because it says that it was found in the vulva, or was it found in a body cavity?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can simply reread what was stated by the forensic doctors: "Red blood at the vulva opening."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is exactly the gist of my question. If blood was exposed to water for two and a half months, would it have decayed, dissolved, would there be chemodialysis, in other words, was it really possible to see traces of red blood on a body on an external part of a body which had spent 2 and a half months under water?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to that question in as much as I am not familiar with the conditions of the preservation of those corpse, I was not present on site, I did not attend the exhumations, I do not have any information in those reports which would enable me to say whether or not the bodies had been immersed in water totally or partially, or what the actual conditions were. Would it be possible for us to have the rest of the text on the screen because there's a portion that is not on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid there is no further mention of the Cirez site beyond these page, but we can try. Unfortunately, I was correct, there is no other document that I could find, including the photos of the victims, the eight women found in the wells. And the last thing that I will try to explore with you, and this has to do with your experience in your long career, have you ever performed autopsies?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in this case, in this particular case or throughout my career?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... during your career because it is clear to me that you were not present there.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, on many times, on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because I assume that you have a lot of experience and we do not, my question relating to the blood issue is regardless of what the assumptions are. So one of the assumptions is that the body was found in a well under water. It was not exhumed. It was taken out of a well where it was immersed. Is it possible then to determine two and a half months later after the body had spent two and a half months under water, is it possible to determine with certainty that there were traces of blood on external parts of the body, or are you unable to give an answer?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the experts who examine the bodies had sufficient information in order to justify the findings that are included in their reports signed by them. Again, if those bodies were indeed removed from a well, I do not have any information to know whether or not the bodies were totally immersed, partially immersed, what was the level of water, and what was their situation compared to others. I don't have the information which would enable me to answer in a precise fashion a fairly general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you of the cross-examination that was conducted by Mr. Visnjic in the Milutinovic case, page 10.178 of the transcript, where in answer to my colleague's question, which was: "On what basis did your colleagues, the French team, conclude that these persons had drowned?" And you replied to my colleague, and I will try to para-phrase your answer, that in the documents that you had reviewed, there is no description of the method in which this was established and how it was determined, so that you cannot answer with certainty what it was that guided your colleagues when they concluded that the cause of death was drowning. In other words, that there was no written evidence to that effect. This claim that you stated, as I presented it now, is this something that you still stand by when we are speaking of the Cirez site?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And I support what was stated in the reports of the forensic experts, because I have no reason to doubt their competence nor their findings. I based those comments on the documents that I was given, the reports, and I myself did not have access to the victims' bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question to do with Cirez is as follows: Can you agree with me that there is no written trace, any written documents in the documents that you reviewed when assessing this site, what the method was used to observe the body -- the traces of blood on the bodies of the two victims, that this was just a claim and nothing else? In other words, that there was no explanation as to how this was determined and what the method applied was?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can confirm there, what you've just said that is that there were no information whereby we could determine whether or not the blood mentioned by the experts was verified in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, your answer is not no, it is yes; it has not been actually checked, there is no evidence that this was in fact traces of blood, if I'm correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. My answer was: In the reports, I did not find any information which would enable me to state that the verification was carried out, but that does not mean that it wasn't done. I simply said that there was no mention of it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is the reply that I expected. Thank you, Doctor. Now I would like you to explain something. You mentioned injuries, that these individuals for -- which were allegedly sexually abused, that there were certain bruises in the vicinity or around the sexual organs. The entries that you mentioned, I assume, were taken from the document that you had at your disposal. You did not have photographs, am I correct? Or were there photographs attached to the documents?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did have photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, the bruises that were observed in the immediate vicinity of the sexual organs, were they of such nature that it can be established without any doubt in both cases of the two victims, that they were caused exclusively and only by a sexual assault on these victims, or is it possible that these bruises were inflicted in some other way?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I noted the existence of these lesions, and I am not able to draw any conclusions. I can simply say that the hypothesis that was referred to, that is, sexual attacks, is compatible, is consistent with that hypothesis. There could be other explanations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question relating to Cirez, the question that I just put, was precisely because of your conclusion that you set forth in your addendum, and now it is completely clear to me after what you've said to me and the Trial Chamber. You state there, and that's on page 2, the third paragraph: "After having reviewed these reports, my opinion is the following: The cause of death is asserted by the French forensic pathologist as an ante mortem drowning. In their report it is not mentioned if complementary analysis had been performed, and the absence of those allow only diagnosis assumptions." In fact, this is the main point after a report of this type without the documents which describe the analysis that had been performed, which according to me would be required for any forensic examination. And in this case, they were missing, or, in other words, you have no evidence or at least you did not see any proof that these bodies had been explored in such a way that all -- that would point to the fact that these autopsies were performed and all analysis as required were actually followed. Is this what I can conclude from your conclusion in the addendum?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, I didn't quite understand your question. What is your question? Of course I can give you once again the conclusion I wrote. There are no other comments I want to make over and beyond what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [In French] I will explain. [In B/C/S] You said in your report that if there are no further analysis, or actually I have not seen them, the only thing that is possible is diagnosis assumption. So that is the gist of my question. Do you stand by what you said there?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said indeed that there had been no supplementary examinations or at least that there had been no mention of extra examinations in the reports conducted by the experts trying to establish the causes of death. As for the possibility of sex abuse, which had been mentioned in the expert report, I clearly indicated that the combination of a number of criteria meant that it was possible. I said there was a compatibility of the elements and of that conclusion. I was in no position and I would in no way dare to establish a conclusion on the basis of pictures and photos. I only said it was compatible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is quite clear, Doctor. What I would like to know is not just the possibility that the case -- that this was a case of sexual abuse, but also whether these persons had drowned or the cause of death was not drowning but perhaps something else. And this is the question that I put in the context of another very important fact, which is the following: That this examination was not accompanied by analysis and proof on the basis of which we could conclude with certainty that the cause of death of these women was drowning?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your line of reasoning. I understand your question. Unfortunately, the elements I have at my disposal are autopsy reports and still photographs. I cannot bring extra information over and beyond what I have written in my own observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, this is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please pull up document -- the first page of document 65 ter 00249.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe we do not have a French translation. But let me say this: This is the first page of a forensic report that was prepared by the Ministry of Defence of the armed forces of the Institute of Pathology in Washington, DC, in the USA. And from the title you can see that this was a "Forensic Examination and Analysis of Human Remains Recovered During a Joint FBI-AFIP Task Force to Assist the International War Tribunal in the Indictment of Kosovo President Milosevic." That's exactly what it says there. I know that you are a forensic expert, but in view of the fact that you had access to all these documents, I believe that there were at least ten expert teams working on this particular case who dealt with human remains and examined human remains at various sites in Kosovo of which you also report in your report. So what I would like to ask you is this: Were there other teams except other than this one where there was a request to get this type of support or assistance in performing the examinations as in the case of President Milosevic? And I assume that this case relates to the former president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Slobodan Milosevic. Do you have -- according to your information, do you know that any other team had this type of explicit request as stated here in this report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. I'm not -- are you talking about the teams that are mentioned in my report, because in that case, you will find the list in my report. But I believe this issue has already been looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: Were these team ad hoc teams or were they actually hired by the ICTY, do you have any knowledge as to that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of this American team, what you observed and what you also noted in your report, and I believe in your report this was on -- this was item 2.5, paragraph 2.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this can be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And I believe this deals with the Milos Gilic Street in Djakovica site. Have you found that in your report, Doctor? When you find it or rather, when I find it -- all right, here I have it.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And then when you look at the next page, we have paragraph 2532 "Status of Bodies." It says there that the human remains constituted of body parts and more or less badly burned skeletal elements. For some of them there were signs of postmortem animal activity. What I would like to ask you is this: Did you have access and did you have any information based on the report compiled by your colleagues from Washington on how burnt these skeletal elements were, what was the degree of their burnt status?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection, no specific recollection, of the state in which these remains had been badly burnt. I can see in my report it says "more or less," basically meaning that there were varied degrees of calcination. I think we should refer back to the pictures that must have illustrated the autopsy reports to get a clearer understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will have to remind you of your conclusion, and please, take a moment to read it. It says 255 -- conclusion from 25 to 27 May -- badly burnt and skeletonised body parts took place in Djakovica. That's what you say. You say "badly burnt." Have you found that portion?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Considering what it says here, "badly burnt and skeletonised body parts," can you explain to us, who are not experts, in the simplest possible words what it really means, this formulation, badly burnt and skeletonised, in some lay terms which we can all understand. Does it mean more or less from what it says here?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the decay and the degradation must have been significant. Indeed there was a fragmentation and some degree of burn of these human remains. In any instance, the impact must have been such that the pathologists were not in a position to establish the cause of death or to establish injuries. So I am assuming that the preservation, the state in which it had been preserved, was very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you've mentioned that, I have another question. Does it mean that the skeletal remains of the bodies of the victims who got hurt are so damaged that not even the examination of these skeletal remains were able to confirm the cause of death, so has the damage been so grave?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is indeed the sense I got when I read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've got a next question. I suppose that your rich expertise is related with accidents. If I'm not mistaken, you mentioned some of your expertise you've exercised in the Mont Blanc tunnel. And I think that most people got asphyxiated, but some of them got burnt because, from your rich practice, there probably were some experiences where people got completely burnt. Have you got some experience that would tell you at what kind of temperature these bodies would have to be exposed for the remains to be so damaged so that even from the skeleton you cannot determine the cause of death and similar issues?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel that whenever an expert is in no position to establish the cause of death or to identify injuries, whatever they may be, any hypothesis might be acceptable and used to establish the cause of death. But I have no specific information enabling me to focus on one reason or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question which is actually the last question for you today and for those of you listening to your answers. And this question relates to the role of experts who is usually part of the team of forensic experts during exhumations. Their role is there to, as you said, to identify the sex, age, and some other characteristics. And these are, you probably have figured it by now, anthropologists. Dear Doctor, on such kind of team, when we talk about expertise and professionalism, can an anthropologist be only a part of the team, or can an anthropologist also lead such a forensic team, or is it something that is intolerable when it comes to basic forensic reasons and assumptions? Do you think that a forensic team could only be guided by a doctor, somebody from a medical profession as a pathologist?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have mentioned this already in my answers yesterday. I explained what the respective roles of the pathologist and the expert forensic pathologist -- anthropologist --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is when the forensic anthropologist is examining human remains of which -- on which there were no longer any soft tissues. In that instance, the anthropologist can contribute to the establishment of the cause of death. Now, in a team made up of a number of experts coming from different fields, it is for the pathologist to come to a conclusion and synthesise all the elements he gets and it is for the pathologist to sign off the autopsy report and the conclusions. At least that is accepted international practice. This being said, the anthropologist does make a significant contribution and a valuable contribution when we are dealing only with skeletal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Doctor. That was my final question. [In English] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Kravetz, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Baccard, yesterday you were asked a series of questions by my learned colleague regarding the distance from which a shot was fired that caused the death of an individual. And in response of one of these questions - and this is at page 7710 - you said that when a shot was fired at close range there would be an imprint on the bone and not on the skin. I wanted to know, when you are examining skeletal remains, how are you able to determine that the imprints that you found -- find or are able to observe on these remains were in fact caused by gun-shot and not by another type of object or another type of impact on the bone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I did not say that when there was a shot fired at short range that there was an imprint on the skull. I said that it was at a touching range when the gun is on the bone, that is in only those circumstances, that when the gun is touching the skin that when there is a gun-shot, the skin lifts off the bone and the gun powder goes and leaves an imprint, a tattoo as we call it, on the bone. As for your specific question, it is a fairly general question, and I'm not sure I know how I could answer your question. As we now know, I did not examine the bodies myself, I worked on the basis of reports and photos --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Doctor, if I can just interrupt you. It was meant to be a general question. And I'm just asking in general terms, when examining skeletal remains, how you are able to distinguish what you've referred to as a tattoo on the bone was caused by a gun-shot and not by another type of object or some other type of trauma on the bone. Is there something particular about these -- what you've referred to as imprints on the bone that would lead you to the conclusion when examining a skeletal remains that these were caused by gun-shot and not by blunt force trauma or by another type of object? That is my question. So it's a general question, not specifically related to the sites that are discussed in your report.

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. There are a number of criteria which can be used in order to describe these imprints, these tattoo marks. There's the morphology itself; there is the distribution of these tattoos these marks, which can either be concentric, asymmetrical, equally distributed compared to the centre point; and there are other examinations that can be carried out on the tissue, in this case the bone tissue, under microscope, for example, but there's also physio chemical test that can be carried out. There are numerous methods that are available that can make it possible to make a differentiated diagnosis on the basis of the traces that have been found.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Doctor, I have a quite similar question. If there are bodies found with wounds of gun-shots, is it possible that there are other causes of death, for instance, heart attack before the shot was made? Can you exclude these possibilities that a certain cause of death had occurred, in these cases generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. First of all -- first of all, the bullet wound itself, how serious is it, as I explained yesterday. If the projectile has hit an important organ in the body, such as the heart, the major vessels, the brain, even if the individual by hypotheses had had a heart attack just a few seconds before, that would only play a secondary part in the death. You have to have an overview, an overall approach in forensic medicine, and start by applying principles of common sense and then a descending range of seriousness, if you will. During the autopsy, an autopsy is carried out not only in the area that has been hit by the projectile, but a full examination which makes it possible to determine whether or not there still remains soft tissue in some of the organs, whether arteries have been blocked, vessels, the heart, for example, if the heart can still function at macroscopic level. All of these aspects make it possible to eliminate the role of another mechanism, be it secondary or accessory, in the cause of death. All of these things are examined by the forensic doctor during the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Doctor, I shall like to refer you to the use of the term "ante mortem" and "peri mortem." Now, are they synonyms, can they be used interchangeably, or are they in two separate and distinct categories, so you have ante mortem, peri mortem, and postmortem?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very good question, Your Honour. I already responded partially yesterday when I spoke about this matter. In my opinion, it is justified to use the word peri mortem in preference to the term ante mortem because the expression "ante mortem" could include events that might have occurred the very day of death, but in the morning, for example, and could lead to confusion with events that took place in the moments surrounding the death. Therefore, today it is generally accepted that the preferable term is "peri mortem" and not "postmortem" because that could include injuries after death such as animal scavengers that have begun deteriorating the body or damaged caused by exhumation using a crane or a digger machine or whatever, a shovel, which can be differentiated very clearly in particular. As regards fractures, that can be differentiated with fractures that occurred at the same time as death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So the bottom line is there are three distinct categories?

utterances.speaker: ERIC BACCARD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be justified to distinguish three different categories indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Doctor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm happy to tell that you that concludes the questioning. The Chamber has very much appreciated your assistance and your attendance again here at The Hague. We would like to thank you for that. We have your report and its annexes to consider. That will take us quite sometime when we come to it. You may, of course, now return to your normal activities, and the Court Officer will assist you. Thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz, the next witness, I take it, is ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is Mr. Keri c. And Mr. Stamp will be leading him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the time. I think it may be a practical course to have the break now and then resume with the fresh witness at 10 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour. I see Mr. Stamp is here. If you want to start with the next witness is also fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems that we can continue now. So we will have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the next witness enters, I would like to ask you to give us a permit or the consent so that my colleague can start with the cross-examination at the beginning and we have filed a written brief on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber is certainly prepared to allow Mr. Popovic to cross-examine this witness. We would add further, in view of what you have put before us before today in respect of the qualifications and experience of both Ms. O'Leary and Mr. Popovic, you need not again move to have either of them deal with the witness. The Chamber will give its standing approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Stamp has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. And good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, could you please start by stating your name and date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: My name is Djordje Keric. I was born on the 16th of May, 1953, in Liplje, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I understand, Mr. Keric, that you are a retired police officer in the MUP of Serbia. Can you briefly describe your career, just tell us where you started and the posts that you held, and the dates when you held those posts until the time of your retirement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: I attended secondary school of Internal Affairs which I completed in Sremska Kamenica by Novi Sad 1972. After that, I was assigned to work in the Secretariat of the Interior in Uzice. And in Uzice, I mainly worked, with some interruptions, until 1993. And I worked there on different duties and activities, starting from a police officer, and I was also a commander of the police station, head of some sectors in the Secretariat, and so on. I was also head of the Secretariat of the Interior in Pristina, and I was attending head of Secretariat in Uzice, and after that I was a special advisor between 1999 in the Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs in Belgrade, that was as of the 1st of May, 1999. And I was also assistant head of the traffic police administration in the MUP of Serbia in Belgrade. And I assumed that position on January the 1st, 2000, and I was retired holding that position on the 1st of July, 2002. So in brief, this would be my career from the beginning until the retirement. Apart from the education I've mentioned, I also attended a school of security in Belgrade. First grade and the second grade in Skopje. It's a high university institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the period of your tenure as SUP chief for Pristina in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: The chief of SUP in Pristina is a position I assumed between the 1st of August, 1994, up until 23rd of June, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when were you appointed the head of the SUP Uzice after that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: I was appointed acting chief of Uzice after I came from the Pristina. It was on the 23rd of June, 1997. And I stayed there before I was appointed to work in the Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs and that was on the 1st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. As chief SUP Uzice, can you recall what were the OUPs or the department of the interior that were subordinate to Uzice Secretariat of Interior?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: In the Uzice SUP we had the following departments: The police department, uniform police; crime police department; traffic police department; general and legal affairs department; fire protection department, and that's it. These are the main departments we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I didn't express the question precisely enough. What were the territorial departments of interior that were subordinate to your SUP?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: I understood your question. Territorial organisation was organised by municipalities and these were OUPs and police stations. If it's a smaller municipality, there we had a police station. General duty police station or traffic police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you name them, the OUPs that were subordinate to your SUP?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Department of interior were in the territory of Uzice and, if I remember well, we had one in Pozega, one in Bajina Basta, in Priboj, Prijepolje, Novo Varos, and Ivanica. And in terms of police stations, we had them in the municipalities of Ciatina [phoen] and Kosjec [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to April 1999. And firstly, can you recall in April 1999 an event in which some bodies were located in -- floating in Lake Perucac came to your attention? In which bodies, human bodies, were found floating in Lake Perucac?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, and of course with the passage of time I've forgotten some, but about 15 days or two weeks before I was transferred to other duties in a different ministry - as I already mentioned, to Belgrade and the Federal Ministry of the Interior - one day, and I can't recall the exact date, I received a call from the chief of OUP Bajina Basta Mr. Slavko Petrovic. He informed me that floating objects were seen on the surface of the lake and that these objects appeared to be human bodies. When I received this information, I ordered that he go to the site to verify the report they received and then to inform me whether these were actually human bodies or some other objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you go on --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Perucac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I was about to ask you that. What was the name of the lake?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Lake Perucac. And this lake is some 10 kilometres from the Bajina Basta OUP. Petrovic went to the spot. And after about an hour, he informed me that five to six human bodies were floating, indeed, on the surface of Lake Perucac, as far as he could tell, from the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where were you when he contacted you the first time and the second time to report that the bodies were in fact floating on the lake?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: I was in my office all this time. My office was in Uzice at this time. I believe that because of the air-strikes, we were relocated. And I was in that office when he called me both times, the first time and the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when he told you that human bodies were in fact floating on the lake, did you tell him anything or give him any further instructions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: After I received this information that these were human bodies, I called my superior in the chain of command, my superior at the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia, I informed him of this extraordinary event, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, who was the acting head of public security at this time in Belgrade. I told him what I had been told by the chief Slavko Petrovic and I sought further instructions, whether we should inform the investigating judge and a prosecutor and I asked for his instructions as to what we were to do next. At this point in time Djordjevic, as far as I can recall, ordered that the chief of the crime police go to the site in order to conduct an on-site investigation together with a group of inspectors, that he should take the necessary measures, and that I should keep him informed subsequently of -- and receive instructions as to what to do afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you told him what you had been told by Petrovic and you sought instructions, whether you should inform the investigating judge and prosecutor. Did Mr. Djordjevic say anything in respect to this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: In respect of this, he just said that I shouldn't inform anyone at this point in time until facts can be checked and the information received from the chief of the crime police Zoran Mitricevic that we should probably secure the site and that later I should contact him and -- once Zoran Mitricevic has been on site and conducted the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was Mitricevic? He was chief of the crime police of which department or which office?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Zoran Mitricevic was the chief of the crime police department in the Uzice Secretariat. And as such, he was in charge both territorially of all the crime police departments in this area, including Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having received these instructions from Mr. Djordjevic, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Mitricevic and a group of inspectors were sent to check the report, and he was supposed to give us feedback, which he did. And after a while, after he had gone on site to the Perucac dam, he informed me, and I can't recall exactly what time of day this was, but he said that the number of bodies was growing and that also there was a case, or rather, a container that was also -- that also surfaced on the body [as interpreted]. He also informed me that the bodies that had appeared on the surface were in an advanced state of decay, that there were no indicators that could lead one to the conclusion where these bodies had come from, who had brought them to the lake, and what the reason for their transport of these bodies to the lake was. And he requested further information and instructions as to what he was to do next. Following this, I called --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you get to that call, just could you tell us exactly what he said to you. I don't think the transcript has down fully what you said Mr. Mitricevic reported to you. What did he tell you about the number of the bodies and what did he tell you was also at the lake?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: As to the number of the bodies, he said that the number compared to the first information that was received that there were five to six bodies, that the number was increased that there some ten -- several tens of bodies, several scores of bodies, and that they were mostly dressed in civilian clothes, that they were in a state of decay, and that a number of bodies were also noted -- that they observed in the container that was -- that also surfaced on the lake surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he describe what type of container it was?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: He did not provide a detailed description. He just said that it was a type of container, a semi-trailer that would be attached to a truck. There were no markings on this, as far as I can recall he did not mention that there were registration plates on it or anything else that could lead to the conclusion as to where the truck had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By what means did he contact you incidentally? How did he contact you from the scene at Lake Perucac?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: He phoned me because there is a police department in Perucac. Whether he called from there or from a civilian line, I really wouldn't know. But he informed me of these events over the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said after you received this information from him, you called someone. Who did you call? And tell us exactly what was said as you recall it.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: As on several previous occasions when I was informed that the number of bodies was increasing, I informed Mr. Djordjevic of this again. I told him that the number of bodies was growing and that there was also a number of bodies in this semi-trailer on the lake, and I sought further instructions from him. And Mr. Djordjevic told me that we would speak a little later. And after about an hour I called him again, as instructed. I think it could have been an hour when I called him again. And he told me then that it was necessary to take measures to remove the bodies from the lake, to engage a number of officers and civilians for this purpose, and that these bodies should be buried in a mass grave near Lake Perucac dam. I conveyed the instructions to the crime police department, Zoran Mitricevic, and they remained on site at the dam some two days during which they were recovering the bodies from the lake and burying them in the vicinity of the dam. Throughout this period, those two days, I never went to the Perucac dam for two reasons. For one, I was preparing for my transfer to other duties and I could not get involved in it; and secondly, this was the time of intense air-strikes because there are numerous military installations in our area, so we had other tasks which took priority in securing and saving citizens and their property in these conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keric. Your Honours, I wonder if this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Stamp. We must have a break now while tapes are rewound. The Court Officer will show you from the court and assist you during the break. We resume again at 4.15. Quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Keric, you said that over the next two days after you first heard about this, the discovery of the bodies, the men remained on the spot under Zoran Mitricevic to retrieve the bodies and to bury them in the mass grave. During that two-day period, did you speak with Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: In those two days, I spoke with Mr. Djordjevic on several occasions requesting further instructions regarding the situation with the recovery of the bodies and their burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was in the -- by the same means, by telephone, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: I communicated with Mr. Djordjevic via a direct phone line in Belgrade. In other words, yes, we communicated by phone on each of these occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If I could take you back to the first time when you phoned him to report to him what the OUP chief Petrovic had told you. Can you recall as closely as possible, or tell us as closely as you can recall, what Mr. Djordjevic said when he heard about these bodies, and if he said what was to be -- or tell us exactly what he said as far as you recall.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, although a lot of time has passed since, the report that some bodies appeared came as a surprise to him, judging by his tone of voice. And I think he said something to the effect that this wasn't good, that it wasn't right. But he did seem surprised when he heard that bodies appeared on Lake Perucac near the Perucac dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you spoke to him that time and you proposed informing the prosecutor and the investigating judge, and he told you not to do so until checks remained, do you recall if he ever gave you any instructions after that in respect to the judge or the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I asked him twice about informing others further on. The first time when the bodies surfaced, when Petrovic informed me, and the second time I asked him whether I should inform the investigating judge when the crime police chief Zoran Mitricevic told me that the number of bodies was increasing and that there was a number of bodies in the semi-trailer. On the second occasion, this was some -- an hour later or so, and I was told then not to advise either the investigating judge or the prosecutor, but rather, to take measures to recover these bodies and bury them near the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why did you propose that you should contact the investigating judge and the prosecutor? I know it sounds like a silly question in the context of things, but could you tell us within the framework of Serbian law and regulations, why did you make that proposition when you heard about these bodies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Well, I proposed it because the standard procedure was in each case, especially where suspicious bodies and deaths occurred, where there are indications that a criminal act is involved, and even in traffic accidents which have serious consequences, the standard procedure is to inform the investigating judge who would then go to the scene and order that an investigation be conducted and other measures be taken to shed light on what had happened, what the causes are, and who the perpetrators might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on the second occasion when you spoke to Mitricevic, did he tell you any further details about the bodies? You said that he told you that there were several tens of bodies, did he tell you any further details about the ages or the sex or the ethnicity of these human bodies that were located?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Mitricevic informed me that all the bodies were in an advanced state of decomposition, and he also advised that there were female and male bodies, and that there were no other indicators that could help to establish where the bodies had come from and where they had been brought from. He could not tell me either, I repeat this, what the purpose was and why it was ordered that this should be done the way it was ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if I may go back to the issue with the investigating judge, there's something I forgot to ask you about that. Did you speak to the investigating judge about this matter in any case?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: In a private conversation about a day or two later, after the completion of this thing, and I can't tell you exactly what day this was, I informed the investigating judge, Mr. Momcilo Krivokapic what had happened, about the appearance of these bodies, and that we did not inform either him or the Prosecutor on orders from the ministry. He had nothing to say to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you form an impression as to whether or not he was aware that this had occurred before you told him?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: No, but there were already public remarks and all kinds of guesses as to whether these bodies were actually the bodies of air-strike victims, because this river flows from Bosnia and through Bajina Basta. And for a while we were wondering whether these bodies may have been exhumed from some grave in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At this time no one could suspect that these were bodies from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if, while you were in Uzice, an investigation was done by the Prosecutor or the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I heard that after I left, which means after May 1st, 1995, when I was transferred to the Federal Ministry of the Interior, I heard that at some point in time somewhat later there was an investigation conducted, that bodies exhumed, and other measures taken in order to establish the facts. However, I was not in that area after this. And after I left, I did not discuss this with anyone, neither the bodies -- I didn't discuss or talk about the bodies, or the exhumation, or any investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, you said after you left on May 1st, is it 1999 you meant? That is when you were transferred into --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And after you left Uzice to take up your new post, can you indicate approximately when next you heard about the events or these events that you just described?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: The first time after I assumed a new position, I heard something about that case from the media. To be more specific, I learned something from Novosti, the most sold daily in Serbia, where there was an article under the name "Water Grave." And in that article for the first time there was some mention of the refrigerator truck holding bodies of Albanian nationals from Kosovo and Metohija. And I think that the article was published in the month of July 2001. I have a copy somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that there was an investigation. Did you -- were you asked to give a statement in the course of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: No, no special statement was required. I read from the media that some exhumation was done, and in 2003 I was invited by Mr. Dilparic, an investigating judge of the special war crime court, and then I gave a statement on everything I knew about the corpses floating on the Perucac lake. Before that, before 2003, I was also invited by the Working Group of the MUP, Ministry of Interior in Belgrade, in Kineza Milosa Street 101 where I gave the first statement on the same issue. In this Working Group, Draga Karleusa was there, he was part of the public security department at the time. Also there was an inspector called Inspector Tadic and another inspector whose name I cannot recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we bring up P394.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is an Official Note of the Working Group. This is an Official Note of the Working Group dated 11th of July, 2001. And it describes the results of their inquiries and interviews up to then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do we have it before us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that you've had a look at it recently and there are a couple of comments that you wanted to make about some of the items we see there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2 of the B/C/S, and if we stay on page 1 of the English. And scroll down to the bottom of page 1 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you wanted to comment on the last paragraph -- or the first paragraph of page 2 in the B/C/S, which would be the penultimate paragraph on page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Somewhere on the top of the paragraph in Serbian it says that there was some previous agreement with myself and an Inspector Dogandzic, and it says that allegedly he suggested hiring divers to sank them. I don't know what this "sanking" means -- "sinking" means, and I didn't have any conversation on that topic with Mr. Dogandzic at the point in time because direct communication that I had was with the bosses, and that was Zoran Mitricevic, chief of crime police; and Slavko Petrovic, who at the time was acting head of the interior department of our OUP in Bajina Basta. Everything else that I discussed, I discussed with them, not with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move on to page 2 of the English. And I think that's page 3 of the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could read the first paragraph on that page and let us have your comment on that, if that is what you remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This first paragraph, Your Honours, is the third -- is in the English -- Are we on page 2 of the English? If you could go down further. Yes, it's the paragraph beginning with the words: "According to Slavko Petrovic ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, if you could comment on that part?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: It says here that during the operation, according to Slavko Petrovic, there was pressure from the MUP of Serbia which was done over the phone by the then chief of the Uzice SUP. But there were no orders in order to speed up the work. And the way it is stated here seems to me that somebody directly called Slavko Petrovic from the ministry or somebody else, because there was no need for us to speed it up because we did have the arrangements with the head of the security department. And it was done according to his instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you had sent Mr. Mitricevic, the crime police chief for the SUP, down. Do you know if he reported along his lines, his specialist lines of command?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: In cases of that type, whenever there's some extraordinary circumstances and some extraordinary consequences, the practice usually was that Mr. Mitricevic, as chief of crime police in the SUP, had to inform his direct superior. And at that time, that was the head of the crime police of the Ministry of the Interior. And at that point that was General Dragan Ilic. I don't know exactly what happened, but I know on the basis of other cases, and earlier cases, that almost on every occasion Mr. Mitricevic was obliged to inform the general in the Ministry of Interior on the measures to be taken in the pre-criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Keric, I wish to move on to something else now, to show you some documents that -- from your position, your former position, you would be familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up 65 ter 5305. Perhaps if you could scroll to the end then and go back to the beginning. Could we look at the second page, at the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this document in general terms. What is the purpose of this document and from whom did it originate?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: This is a usual document. It's a fax which was sent from the level of the Ministry of Interior, the republic one, to the Secretariat of the Interior, or Secretariats rather. In every case, when a certain number of people were assigned or deployed to apply special security measures or undertake special security tasks. In any case, this document describes forces to be deployed in Kosovo and Metohija for special security measures when there were assignments made by Secretariats, by SUPs, which Secretariats should do what, how many people should be sent, and which equipment should be sent in order carry out security measures in Kosovo and Metohija. In this particular case, the Secretariat in which I worked is not mentioned. Other Secretariats are mentioned in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you identify who signed it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: The document was signed by the public security department head, chief of the public security department Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, in the case of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know his signature?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say, although we used to receive such documents whenever there was some deployment of forces in the area of Kosovo. And we received such documents every forty days where there was some re-assignment and rotation of personnel. In most cases, such orders, such documents, were signed by the commander of Special Forces of the police, PJPs, and that's Obrad Stevanovic. Because it was under his competence to train -- to train the staff and everybody working in PJPs. And he had special authorities in that respect with regard to his direct superior and that was the chief of the public security department. In this case, in this particular case, I could see that Mr. Djordjevic signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could this document 5305 be received in evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was a mistake in what is the response -- was put in, with an error. So let us correct that. It says that the boss of the public security department. And I think that the reply of the witness was a different one to whom he was directly responsible, that was the question. And can we just clear that out because I think that's important because I don't want any confusions to be made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was, To whom was Obrad Stevanovic accountable. I think he was directly accountable to the minister of the interior, at that time the minister of interior in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you wanting it received now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, yes, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01181.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to 65 ter number 5306. And when it comes up, could we look quickly at the first page and the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a similar order to the last one we discussed from the chief of the public security department deploying PJP personnel to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Well, I think this is the same. It's a usual common document which was usually sent after every rotation of people who left or people who came back from the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could this be received as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01182.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at 5307. This one is now dated 8th of January, 1999. Could we look at the first and then the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that is, just briefly, if it's the same as before?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: As in the previous two documents, this is an order to send out a certain number of people as it is set in the document, to carry out some tasks in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. In this document, as in the previous one, it describes Secretariats Belgrade, Nis, Vranje, where I didn't work. My Secretariat is not in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could this one be received as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01183.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 5308, could we bring up that one, please. And move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what that is, please, Mr. Keric?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: This is also an order to send a certain number of people, mainly police officers, in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. And the numbers shown here include Uzice SUP where the role of the Secretariat in Uzice was for the police officer to prepare the people, to inform the people, who by day line of work were part of the special units, to gather them, and to notify them about the time and place, when and where they will be deployed. Everything else, the logistic support, the equipment and arms, were provided by the command of the PJPs from the ministry in Belgrade by was run by the General Obrad Stevanovic. And there is a bus which was sent from the Ministry of the Interior to take over people from the Uzice Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically receiving this one?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall specifically. I see that it happened on the 21st of January, 1999. But when we received these document, they are signed off, and they are given to competent police officers from the particular department who then followed up on that with the technical preparations and specific tasks in line with the orders provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to avoid confusion in the future, this is the 14th of January, I see on the screen here. That's what you meant, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I read that the first rotation ends on the 21st of January, but you are right. Sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this one be received, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just have a remark about the copy. On the copy I have there is no signature on the document. Can we take a look at the document in the e-court, whether there is a signature there, because if there is no signature and the witness does not recall specifically -- well, even in the e-court there is no signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no signature by hand, I don't know why, but the contents are the same as in other previous documents. I don't know what happened here, maybe it was a mistake, maybe it wasn't signed, but I don't know specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that be received and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01184.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move to 5310. If we could move to the next page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just briefly, Mr. Keric, tell us the purport and provenance of that document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: This document does not relate to Uzice Secretariat. And the contents and the substance is the same as before, the end of the rotation and the deployment in the area of Kosovo and Metohija of some forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's from the assistant minister in charge of the public security department; is that what you see there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: In this case, the document was signed by the chief of the public security department, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic. Now, let me try and clarify: I know that at some point in time all types of such documents were signed by the commander of the PJPs since those tasks were under the direct competence and authorities. Sometime later, when the security situation changed or became more complex and there were some announcements that an air-strike by the NATO was going to happen, as the time was passing by, then documents were signed by Vlastimir Djordjevic as chief of the public security department. I don't know why it happened like that. I don't know what the segregation of activities or tasks was at the time at the top of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could this document, Your Honours, be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01185.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we now go to 5311.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the 15th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And now on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see there that it's also addressed to the detachments in Uzice. This one is also not signed, the copy we have here, but could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: It is a document of the same substance. The same order is issued as in the previous documents. There is no difference. And I don't really know why it wasn't signed. Also, I didn't manage to see, I didn't see the first part, to see whether it also referred to Uzice SUP or whether these detachments belonged to Uzice. Because the command of the 35th Detachment covered the areas of several Secretariats, Valjevo, Kraljevo, Cacak, Uzice, Novi Pazar, and Sabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: I see Cacak, Novi Pazar, Valjevo, Sabac, and Uzice as well. So the substance is the same as the earlier dispatch. The vehicles are provided for the members of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I think it says in the body that your SUP would provide the ministry -- or the bus; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Exactly. And there are also men from the Uzice Secretariat who are assigned to this task. Also the bus that was provided by the auto repair shop of the Ministry of Interior for the transport of these people from Uzice to Kosovo and Metohija, whatever they were assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could that document be given an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is not on the 65 ter list, Mr. Stamp. It's the subject of a motion to be included in the list. It will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I am sorry. I thought that this one had been disposed of but thanks for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01186 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to 5276. And having regard to what happened with the last document, I must inform Your Honours that I'm not sure if this one was disposed of by the Court. That is information I previously had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a very short order cancelling a previous deployment. Can you see that, Mr. Keric? And tell us where this order came from?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Yes. The order came from the ministry, Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, from the public security department. I don't know what it relates to specifically, but some measures are mentioned that had been ordered earlier, in an earlier dispatch, and they are hereby declared no longer valid. But I don't know what these other dispatches, 349, this other dispatch, what it relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be the next document we come to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But could we give 65 ter 5276 an exhibit number, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01187.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that's dated the 23rd of February. There's another document of the 23rd of February, that's 5312. If we could have a look at that one quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think this is an order. Or you could tell us briefly what it is and from where it came?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: The document is a document of the Ministry of the Interior from the public security department, and it deals with the sending and deployment of some members of the Special Police Units to Kosovo and Metohija. It says here that, in this particular case, members of the 35th PJP Detachment were sent to Kosovska Mitrovica which was under the Uzice Secretariat. The same case being as in all the previous dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's from the assistant minister in charge of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: The signature is that of the chief of the public security department, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is dispatch number 349, dated the 23rd of February, 1999. I just ask to note that. Your Honours, could this one also be received in evidence and be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01188.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Something I should have asked you before in respect to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we have a quick look at it. That is 65 ter number P5276. Which is P1187.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's something illogical here. The dispatch number 349 actually removes certain measures that had been ordered previously, whether those were enhanced security measures or some others, I don't know, but they are pronounced no longer valid. And then at the same time it also orders the rotation of certain units and members of units, which, to me, is not quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. But you see here that this dispatch revokes the previous one that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE KERIC
utterances.text: Although I'm doing my best, I can't really figure out what this is about. This should mean that certain measures were revoked. But in the earlier dispatch, there was no -- there were no orders issued. It was just the same type of standard dispatch as the ones that we had seen earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could we move on now to 5288. This is now in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with the deployment of units from other Secretariats, Belgrade and other places, to the area of Kosovo and Metohija to Decani, Pec. And I don't see that there are any members of the Uzice Secretariat in this particular case, in this particular shift. I can't see the next page and the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page and the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see the signature of the assistant minister and the chief of public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm advised that this one is not yet on the exhibit list. But what I'm being told now, Your Honours, and I think subject to correction, I would say it's not yet on the exhibit list, is that the order had been that the Prosecution should provide a translation because at the time of the application or the time of the decision there were no translations of this document. And, indeed, the last one that we discovered was not yet on the exhibit list. But I could check that in the break and advise the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
